summary: This informational RFC describes the IETF architecture for a standard programmatic interface for state transfer in and out of the Internet routing system, covering the high-level architecture, its building blocks and interfaces, with focus on those to be standardized for I2RS.

plainLanguage.summary: I2RS describes a standard way for software to read information from routers and request changes to some router state. This RFC explains the parts of that architecture and how they interact.

questions: interface to the routing system architecture
what is an i2rs agent and client
what is ephemeral state in i2rs
how does i2rs handle conflicting writes
subtitle: How applications can read and write routing-system state through clients and agents.

tldr.problem: Network applications need a common programmatic way to read routing state, receive events, and change forwarding-related state.
tldr.mechanism: I2RS uses clients and agents with data-model-driven asynchronous exchanges for reads, writes, subscriptions, and information collection.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC describes the architecture and security assumptions. It points to separate work for protocol details and requirements.

today: RFC 7921 is an Informational architecture document published in June 2016. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it describes architecture rather than the detailed protocol requirements.

sections.title: The Need for a Programmatic Interface
sections.content:
Routers hold routing, topology, and forwarding information that network applications may need to observe. Applications may also need to install forwarding-related state.

The Interface to the Routing System (I2RS) is an asynchronous, programmatic interface for moving state into and out of the routing system. It supports structured data access, event subscriptions, and ephemeral state that does not survive a routing-element reboot.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications need more than command-line access to routers. I2RS provides a defined way for software to request information and temporary changes.

sections.title: Clients, Agents, and Routing Elements
sections.content:
An application accesses I2RS through a client; the client communicates with an agent that is part of a routing element. A client may serve one or more applications and talk to multiple agents, while an agent may serve multiple clients.

The agent provides read and write access to selected data and lets clients subscribe to event notifications. Communication is asynchronous, so clients and agents can handle multiple requests at once. The architecture covers the client-agent interaction, not how applications connect to a remote client.
sections.plainLanguage: The application uses a client, and the client talks to an agent on the router. One client can serve several applications, and an agent can serve several clients.

sections.title: Simple, Extensible Data Models
sections.content:
The architecture emphasizes simplicity, extensibility, and model-driven interfaces. A large number of possible data items and operations could make the protocol complex, so the RFC recommends including complexity only when needed.

Data models describe the information and its meaning. Clients and agents need implement only the models they use or support, and tools can help check and manipulate modelled data. The architecture also needs ways to represent device variation and relationships between objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Data models give clients and agents a shared description of router information. Each side can support only the models it needs, while the design leaves room for new models.

sections.title: Ephemeral State and Conflicting Changes
sections.content:
The agent keeps track of changes applied for clients and active subscriptions. It retains I2RS changes until a client removes them, another operation overrides them, or the routing element reboots. Removing an I2RS change restores the state that would exist without it.

Local Configuration and I2RS changes are resolved by operator policy and priority, not simply by which change arrived most recently. When clients write the same data, the higher-priority client wins; a tie goes to the client first attributed to that data. The architecture also defines notifications for graceful agent shutdown and restart after failure.
sections.plainLanguage: I2RS changes are temporary and do not return after a reboot. If two clients try to change the same item, the agent uses priority rules rather than relying on timing.

sections.title: Messages, Notifications, and Errors
sections.content:
The architecture assumes data models in YANG 1.1 and names NETCONF and RESTCONF as protocols to be expanded for I2RS. It allows multiple communication channels and transports, with suitable authentication, integrity protection, and congestion control.

Clients can subscribe to filtered event notifications and request snapshots or feeds of changing information. A single message may contain several operations and use one of three error-handling modes: perform all or none, perform until error, or attempt all and report failures. The architecture does not define multi-message atomicity or rollback.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask for data, subscribe to selected events, or send several operations in one message. It can choose how the agent should handle errors in that message.

viz.caption: THREE ERROR-HANDLING MODES FOR ONE MESSAGE

items.title: All or none
items.text: Apply every operation or roll back the operations in the message.

items.title: Until error
items.text: Apply operations in order and stop at the first error.

items.title: Attempt all
items.text: Try every operation and report each failure.
